messages.subject: more data breaks model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I'm having an issue where adding more data to a model breaks it, and I'm at a loss to explain it, so thought I'd ask here!

I have a very large complex integrated population model, which means I can't really provide an example to test, but I will try to explain in as much detail as I can.

The model works with a short test run of data (3 years). It has a fixed effect of site within one survival parameter, all other parameters are constant. I initially had some issues with this model, but after reading some of the forum questions, I changed the samplers for the parameters to slice samplers, as the forum suggests they are better for times when certain parameter values can produce issues. I also truncated the prior to be sure the parameter values could not exceed certain values, as survival ahs to be between 0 and 1 for the model to work:
survival ~ T(dunif(0,1),0,1)
The truncation was necessary to get the short data test run to work, but it runs perfectly.

Having had some success with this I then increased the data going into the model to 10 years worth. Nothing else changed, but I now get loads of warnings and the survival parameters now always exceed the boundary of 0-1 (I had a survival of -438!). It seems clear to me the warnings are resulting from parameters values that just aren't possible within this model. I have no idea how or why the model is overriding the prior and truncation with 10 years of data but not with 3 years worth.

Does anyone have any idea why this might be occurring with only extra data? Or any tips to try and diagnose the issue?

Thanks,
Ellie

messages.body_plain:
It’s hard to diagnose with the error messages - maybe you could take a screenshot or copy a few so we can all see what the errors are?

 My best guess from this limited information is that something upstream is created impossible log-likelihood scenarios and when it comes to estimating the likelihood of the survival parameters it encounters Inf, -Inf and just spits out some random number outside of the bounds. I haven’t seen this with nimble specifically but in JAGS this type of error seemed to be frequent when you have a scenario where you sometimes but not always divide by 0.

-Heather

messages.subject: R Aborting During Sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A few weeks ago I tried Nimble HMC using the beta version of Nimble, and then recently decided to switch back and I reinstalled the current version of Nimble. However, now whenever I go to run sampling on any compiled model, R encounters a fatal error and aborts. R aborts even when running previous versions of models that worked fine a few weeks ago, and on an example model from the Nimble user manual that should have been able to run. I've tried reinstalling R, Rstudio, and Rtools to make sure that everything is up to date, and that failed to solve the issue. Has anyone encountered an issue like this before?

Thanks,
Jen

messages.subject: Re: R Aborting During Sampling
messages.body_plain:
Well, that sounds disconcerting. A few things to check:

1) Let's make sure you have the non-AD-enabled nimble installed. This should return `NULL`:

> nimbleOptions('enableDerivs')

2) What's the exact error message you get when you run the example from the manual (and which example are you running)?

3) Also, to see if your Rtools is working, please try to run a basic Rcpp operation (I'm assuming here that you have Rcpp installed, but you can install it if not):

> Rcpp::cppFunction(
          'int fibonacci(const int x) {
              if (x == 0) return(0);
              if (x == 1) return(1);
              return (fibonacci(x - 1)) + fibonacci(x - 2);
          }')
> fibonacci(7)

-chris

messages.subject: Re: more data breaks model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ellie,

Thanks for posting the question, and thanks Heather for contributing as well.

My guess is that some values are initialized in an invalid way, giving the warnings, which then can have potentially unpredictable behavior during sampling.  If the model has some invalid (NaN or -Inf) log probabilities, everything will go haywire.

It is not clear to me what T(dunif(0,1), 0, 1) will do that is different from dunif(0,1). What am I missing there? If you want to ensure avoidance of the boundaries, my thought would be something like dunif(0.000001, 0.999999).

In models with logit (or probit) links, a common glitch can be initial values that give numerical 0s or 1s.  For example, expit(-1000) is not just a tiny number but exactly 0 to within machine precision. If that is the Bernoulli probability for an outcome that is a 1, it is impossible and will give prob = 0, i.e. log prob = -Inf.  So if the initial values going into a linear combination of predictors (that are then expit-transformed) are too haphazard and happen to make huge negative or positive numbers, it can lead to impossible outcomes in the model, and it may or may not recover in MCMC.  Of course, other pathologies can happen.  Another one in ecological models with sequences of counts involving binomials is to have the size parameter (number of trials) smaller than the x value, again yielding log prob = -Inf.

You can track down where the problems are by using the model as an object.

If you are using nimbleMCMC, switch gears and instead first build the model yourself using nimbleModel, with the same code, data, inits, and constants as you use for nimbleMCMC.  Say the result is `m`.

m$calculate() # See if you have NaN or -Inf, indicating lack of complete and valid inits.
Then track down which variable contains one or more nodes with NaN or -Inf log probs:
m$calculate('y') # sum of log probs of all elements of y in your model
m$calculate('z') # etc, see which variable produces a -Inf.
Then track it down to individual elements
m$calculate('z[1:10]') # sum of log probs of z[1]...z[10], etc
Then look at the input values that enter into whatever log probability is -Inf or NaN.  You can inspect values in the model to find problems using natural R syntax:
m$y
m$z[1:100] # etc.
With luck and sleuthing you might be able to find what values give an invalid log prob calculation.

If you're not providing complete inits, then the problem could arise from the prior draws that will be used by the MCMC prior to the start of sampling.  You can see the result of those if you build and run the MCMC manually and run it for 0 iterations.  This can be done uncompiled or compiled.

In case it's helpful and you haven't already dived in, our user manual and examples tabs at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org> have more thorough examples of how model objects can be used.

If you're still stuck, the best step would be to share a reproducible example.  It can be helpful if you trim out and/or reduce the size of parts of the model that aren't needed, even if makes it scientifically silly, if it's easy to do so (not always the case).  You can share it off-list if it involves data you'd prefer not to post.

Here was a thread from October 2022 that might be relevant: https://groups.google.com/u/2/g/nimble-users/c/MVonZE9QolY. There may be other relevant threads too.

HTH

Perry

In the code below, I would like to use RJMCMC

Code <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:S){
    y[1:N,i] ~ dmnorm(mu_y[1:N, i], prec = tau_y0[1:N, 1:N, i])
     mu_y[1:N, i] <- b[i, 1] * x1[1:N] + b[i, 2] * x2[1:N] + b[i, 3] *
      x3[1:N] + b[i, 4] * x4[1:N] + b[i, 5] * x5[1:N]
    tau_y0[1:N, 1:N, i] <- diag(psi_y[i] * exp(-Dist[1:N, i]/lambda))

    for (j in 1:5) {

      b[i, j] ~ dnorm(0, tau)

    }

    b0[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    psi_y[i] ~ dgamma(1, 1)

  }

  gamma1~ dbern(psi)
  gamma2~ dbern(psi)
  gamma3~ dbern(psi)
  gamma4~ dbern(psi)
  gamma5~ dbern(psi)
  psi ~ dbeta(1, 1)
  lambda ~ dunif(0, D)
  tau ~ dgamma(1, 1)

configureRJ(conf = RJexampleConf,
            targetNodes = ("b"),
            indicatorNodes = c('gamma1', 'gamma2',"gamma3","gamma4","gamma5"),

messages.body_plain:
Yes, the error is saying that the RJ target nodes - each of the b[i,j] - cannot have a non-constant hyperparamter.  In this case, that means the non-constant parameter tau, in the prior:

     b[i, j] ~ dnorm(0, tau)

So you would need a prior more similar to:

     b[i, j] ~ dnorm(0, 1)

Also, are you sure you want b[i,j] to be indexed by "i"?  Just looking at your code, I feel like only having b[j] for j=1..5 might be what you're after.

Good luck,
Daniel

messages.subject: Reminder: BDM workshop June 1-2nd 2023 MUSC Charleston USA
messages.subject_clean: Reminder: BDM workshop June 1-2nd 2023 MUSC Charleston USA
messages.body_plain:
Just a few places remain for the workshop:

Using R for Bayesian Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Health Modeling

Parts I, II

June 1st – 2nd 2023

COURSE CONTENT

These courses are designed to provide a comprehensive introduction to the area of Bayesian disease mapping using R in applications to Public Health and Epidemiology:  Part I will run on June 1st and Part II on June 2nd, 2023.

Part I consists of sessions dealing with:

AM

•            Basic concepts of Bayesian methods and disease mapping

•            Bayesian computation: MCMC and alternatives

PM

•            R graphics for spatial health data

•            Bayesian Hierarchical Models for disease mapping (BHMs):

Simple models:  Poisson-gamma; log-normal, convolution.

Variants: Leroux, mixture, BYM2.

•            Model goodness of fit

•            Demonstration of risk estimation and using BRugs/OpenBUGS

Part II consists of sessions dealing with

AM

•            Nimble

•            CARBayes

•            INLA

PM

•            Space-time modelling with McMC (Nimble)

•            Space-time modelling with INLA

•            Clustering in space and space-time

•            Infectious disease modelling and surveillance

This workshop sequence is designed for those who want to cover mapping methods, and the use of a variety of software and variants in application to small area health data.

The course will include theoretical input, but also practical elements and participants will be involved in hands-on in the use of R, BRugs (OpenBUGS), Nimble, CARBayes and INLA in disease mapping applications.

Both human and veterinary examples will be covered in the course as well as simple space-time modelling.

Examples will range over congenital anomaly birth data, a lung, larynx and oral cancer example, foot and mouth disease in the UK, and influenza and Covid-19 space-time modeling in South Carolina.

THE SPEAKER

Andrew B. Lawson (Department of Public Health Sciences, College of Medicine, Medical University of South Carolina) is a MUSC Distinguished Professor Emeritus and a World Health Organization (WHO) advisor

on Disease Mapping and organized with WHO an international workshop on this topic which has led to an edited volume “Disease Mapping and Risk Assessment for Public Health”.

He recently acted as chief editor of the CRC Handbook of Spatial Epidemiology (2016).

He has published a number of books focused on disease mapping and spatial epidemiology. In particular, the 3rd edition of the book: Lawson, A. B.  Bayesian Disease Mapping  CRC Press, appeared in 2018.

The recent addition:

Lawson, A. B. (2021) Using R for Bayesian Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Health Modeling. CRC Press.

will be a course text for the workshop. A copy of this book is included in the fee for the course.

WHO SHOULD ATTEND

The course is intended for epidemiologists and public health workers who need to analyse geographical disease incidence. In addition, the course sequence may be of interest to statisticians

or geographers and planners who deal with spatial disease data. Some statistical/epidemiological background would be beneficial but not essential. Experience of basic R use is assumed.

WHY ATTEND

Participants will gain an in-depth understanding of the basic issues, methods and techniques used in the analysis of spatial health data using a Bayesian approach on R.

They will gain insight into the detailed analysis of practical problems in risk estimation and cluster detection. The course is presented by an acknowledged expert in the field of disease mapping and spatial epidemiology.

COURSE FEE AND REQUIREMENTS

Booking of the two-day course sequence is $1000.

**Early Bird rate of $600 before May 20th**

Attendees are recommended to pre-load: OpenBUGS (most recent version). Datasets will be provided.  R software can be downloaded

from the following websites: http://cran.wustl.edu OpenBUGS can be downloaded from http://www.openbugs.net/w/Downloads

A variety of R packages will be used in the workshop. The main R packages used will be BRugs, Nimble, CARBayes, and INLA.

The graphics libraries maptools, sp, spdep, sf, tmap, and ggplot2 will also be used.

Additional R packages will be needed, and notification of these will be sent to participants in the joining instructions.

VENUE

This workshop will be hosted by the Medical University of South Carolina, Department of Public Health Sciences, 135 Cannon Street, Charleston, South Carolina. The location of the workshop is TBA.

Registration queries can be made with Paula Talbot (tal...@musc.edu).

Technical queries can be made to Andrew Lawson (laws...@musc.edu)

Registration form at :

https://medicine.musc.edu/departments/phs/news-and-events/upcoming-events/bayesian-workshop-2023

messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much for your thoughts!

I really appreciate having some avenues to explore. I will have a look at all your suggestions and try to feedback whether or not I locate the issue (in case that is useful for others in the future)

To answer a few of your questions quickly:

The errors seem to relate to values that shouldn't be possible. For example:
Warning: slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions for 'mpe'. Current parameter value is -1.11838e+20.
Where 'mpe' is a detection probability that should be between 0 and 1. I will have a close look at the model and data to see if there are any divisions by 0 or other issues for the log-likelihood as Heather suggests.

I don't really understand why T(dunif(0,1), 0, 1)  seemed to make a difference for the short data, but testing dunif(0.000001, 0.999999) for the medium data did not help unfortunately. I will try tracking down any initial value issues, as I know I don't have everything initialised.

Thanks,
Ellie

On Thu, 2 Mar 2023 at 04:30, Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Ellie,
>
> Thanks for posting the question, and thanks Heather for contributing as well.
>
> My guess is that some values are initialized in an invalid way, giving the warnings, which then can have potentially unpredictable behavior during sampling.  If the model has some invalid (NaN or -Inf) log probabilities, everything will go haywire.
>
> It is not clear to me what T(dunif(0,1), 0, 1) will do that is different from dunif(0,1). What am I missing there? If you want to ensure avoidance of the boundaries, my thought would be something like dunif(0.000001, 0.999999).
>
> In models with logit (or probit) links, a common glitch can be initial values that give numerical 0s or 1s.  For example, expit(-1000) is not just a tiny number but exactly 0 to within machine precision. If that is the Bernoulli probability for an outcome that is a 1, it is impossible and will give prob = 0, i.e. log prob = -Inf.  So if the initial values going into a linear combination of predictors (that are then expit-transformed) are too haphazard and happen to make huge negative or positive numbers, it can lead to impossible outcomes in the model, and it may or may not recover in MCMC.  Of course, other pathologies can happen.  Another one in ecological models with sequences of counts involving binomials is to have the size parameter (number of trials) smaller than the x value, again yielding log prob = -Inf.
>
> You can track down where the problems are by using the model as an object.
>
> If you are using nimbleMCMC, switch gears and instead first build the model yourself using nimbleModel, with the same code, data, inits, and constants as you use for nimbleMCMC.  Say the result is `m`.
>
> m$calculate() # See if you have NaN or -Inf, indicating lack of complete and valid inits.
> Then track down which variable contains one or more nodes with NaN or -Inf log probs:
> m$calculate('y') # sum of log probs of all elements of y in your model
> m$calculate('z') # etc, see which variable produces a -Inf.
> Then track it down to individual elements
> m$calculate('z[1:10]') # sum of log probs of z[1]...z[10], etc
> Then look at the input values that enter into whatever log probability is -Inf or NaN.  You can inspect values in the model to find problems using natural R syntax:
> m$y
> m$z[1:100] # etc.
> With luck and sleuthing you might be able to find what values give an invalid log prob calculation.
>
> If you're not providing complete inits, then the problem could arise from the prior draws that will be used by the MCMC prior to the start of sampling.  You can see the result of those if you build and run the MCMC manually and run it for 0 iterations.  This can be done uncompiled or compiled.
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tin,

As you've probably gathered from the lack of response, we don't have any active plans in this area. As far as tutorials, the best I can offer is that you can look at the code for our BNP stuff to see if that gives you any ideas of how to implement things. The code we have for defining the CRP distribution (in `BNP_distributions.R`) is straightforward, while the code for MCMC sampling is in the `BNP_samplers.R` file. These are in our GitHub repository (github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/packages/nimble <http://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/packages/nimble>). I will say the sampling code there is fairly complicated because of all the different ways that people could use CRP formulations in a model and wanting to deal with conjugacy.

Happy to chat further if you decide you want to try to implement something and have questions.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Arjun,

Note that "Error in if (cond) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" appears in relation to the warning about model initialization. I suspect it's coming specifically from the fact that you have not initialized 'v'.

As far as the index out of bounds, please see our example for the stickbreaking specification in our manual (https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-bnp.html#sec:exsb). In particular the output of `stick_breaking` is a set of probabilities not a set of category indicators, so it shouldn't be assigned to `xi`. So you'll need to fix up your model specification to correctly define `xi`.

As far as the -Inf logProb values, that is probably because you haven't initialized something. Please see this post from a while back <https://groups.google.com/u/0/g/nimble-users/c/MVonZE9QolY> where we talk about strategies for debugging cases like this by manipulating the model.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Just in case anyone else comes across this problem, the solution was all about sampler choice. I simply had to tell NIMBLE to jointly sample s[,1:2] (the x and y coordinates of each point) and the error went away. Seems a little foolish now in retrospect.

My solution:
adaptInterval = 200
SamplerScale <- 0.05
mcmcbirds$removeSampler(paste0("s[",1:nind,", 1:2, 1:",nocc,"]"))
for(i in 1:nind){
  for(tt in 1:occ){
    mcmcbirds$addSampler(target = paste0("s[",i,", 1:2, ",tt,"]"),
                         type = 'RW_block', silent=TRUE,
                         control = list(adaptInterval = adaptInterval, propCov=diag(2), scale=SamplerScale, adaptScaleOnly=TRUE))
  }

messages.body_plain:
Hello! I am attempting to simulate from a SIRS model in NIMBLE with a seasonal force of infection (beta[t] in the second set of code below), and all of the random distributions generate NAs (e.g.,  Warning messages: 1: In rbinom(1, size = model$I[getNodeFunctionIndexedInfo(INDEXEDNODEINFO_, ... : NAs produced ) .

The first set of code below does not include a seasonal component and works. The second set is the simplest example I could come up with that throws NA warnings. Do you have any suggestions on how to approach this problem? Thank you in advance for any help you can provide.

Code that works:
SIRS_code <-  nimbleCode({

  S[1] <- N - I0 - R0
  I[1] <- I0
  R[1] <- R0

  probIR <- 1 - exp(-gamma)
  probRS <- 1 - exp(-phi)

  ### loop over time
  for(t in 1:tau) {

    probSI[t] <- 1 - exp(- beta1 * I[t] / N)

    Istar[t] ~ dbin(probSI[t], S[t])
    Rstar[t] ~ dbin(probIR, I[t])
    Sstar[t] ~ dbin(probRS, R[t])

    # update S, I, R
    S[t + 1] <- S[t] - Istar[t] + Sstar[t]
    I[t + 1] <- I[t] + Istar[t] - Rstar[t]
    R[t + 1] <- R[t] + Rstar[t] - Sstar[t]

    # data not perfectly observed
    nu[t] <- logit(Istar[t]/N+0.0001)
    logit(Y[t]) ~ dnorm(nu[t], 0.1)

  }

  # priors
  beta1 ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
  gamma ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
  phi ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
})

n_weeks <- 52
n_seasons <- 2
constantsList <- list(N = 10000,
                      I0 = 5,
                      R0 = 0,
                      tau = n_weeks*n_seasons)

sirsModel <- nimbleModel(SIRS_code,
                         constants = constantsList)

# exclude data from parent nodes
dataNodes <- c('Istar', 'Rstar', 'Sstar', 'logit_Y')
dataNodes <- sirsModel$expandNodeNames(dataNodes, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
parentNodes <- sirsModel$getParents(dataNodes, stochOnly = TRUE)
parentNodes <- parentNodes[-which(parentNodes %in% dataNodes)]
parentNodes <- sirsModel$expandNodeNames(parentNodes, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
nodesToSim <- sirsModel$getDependencies(parentNodes, self = FALSE, downstream = T)

initsList <- list(beta1 = 0.6,
                  gamma = 0.2,
                  phi = 0.1)
sirsModel$setInits(initsList)

set.seed(1)
sirsModel$simulate(nodesToSim, includeData = TRUE)

Minimal example that throws NA warnings:

  S[1] <- N - I0 - R0
  I[1] <- I0
  R[1] <- R0

  probIR <- 1 - exp(-gamma)
  probRS <- 1 - exp(-phi)

  ### loop over time
  for(t in 1:tau) {

    probSI[t] <- 1 - exp(- beta[t] * I[t] / N)
    ## need to add seasonal beta to this next
    beta[t] <- 0.5*(1+0.9*sin((2*pi/52)*(w[t]-52/4)))

    Istar[t] ~ dbin(probSI[t], S[t])
    Rstar[t] ~ dbin(probIR, I[t])
    Sstar[t] ~ dbin(probRS, R[t])

    # update S, I, R
    S[t + 1] <- S[t] - Istar[t] + Sstar[t]
    I[t + 1] <- I[t] + Istar[t] - Rstar[t]
    R[t + 1] <- R[t] + Rstar[t] - Sstar[t]

    # data not perfectly observed
    nu[t] <- logit(Istar[t]/N+0.0001)
    logit(Y[t]) ~ dnorm(nu[t], 0.1)

  }

  # priors
  gamma ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
  phi ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
})

n_weeks <- 52
n_seasons <- 2
constantsList <- list(N = 10000,
                      I0 = 5,
                      R0 = 0,
                      tau = n_weeks*n_seasons,
                      w = rep(1:n_weeks, n_seasons))

sirsModel <- nimbleModel(SIRS_code,
                         constants = constantsList)

# exclude data from parent nodes
dataNodes <- c('Istar', 'Rstar', 'Sstar', 'logit_Y')
dataNodes <- sirsModel$expandNodeNames(dataNodes, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
parentNodes <- sirsModel$getParents(dataNodes, stochOnly = TRUE)
parentNodes <- parentNodes[-which(parentNodes %in% dataNodes)]
parentNodes <- sirsModel$expandNodeNames(parentNodes, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
nodesToSim <- sirsModel$getDependencies(parentNodes, self = FALSE, downstream = T)

initsList <- list(gamma = 0.2,
                  phi = 0.1)
sirsModel$setInits(initsList)

set.seed(1)
sirsModel$simulate(nodesToSim, includeData = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marie,

Thanks for the question and especially the simplified and reproducible example.  That does make it much easier to take a look.

I see two things going on.  The first is that there is some kind of glitch with using the constant 'pi' in the model code.  This shouldn't be the case, so we need to take a look into that.  As a workaround, please replace it with something like "my_pi" and then in your constantsList include "my_pi = pi", so the actual value of pi is inserted into the model as a constant without relying on the special name "pi".

Then I see that even with that workaround, your code throws errors.  I am not completely following what you want to end up with from the model structure queries, but what I can see is that "Istar[1]" is not included in nodesToSim, and having that not simulated seems to set off a cascade of NAs through the time steps of the model.  I was just inspecting with code like:

sirsModel$Y[1]
sirsModel$nu[1]
sirsModel$Istar[1]
sirsModel$S[1]
sirsModel$probSI[1]
sirsModel$w[1]
sirsModel$beta[1]
sirsModel$I[1]
constantsList$w[1]

This issue was undoubtedly somewhat masked from your debugging efforts by the problem with pi, so I am hoping you'll be able to work out what you want from here.  I wonder if some of the options in model$getNodeNames would be helpful, e.g. "topOnly = TRUE" will give all the nodes with no stochastic parents.  Is something like setdiff(sirsModel$getNodeNames(), c("gamma", "phi")) useful?

HTH.
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am new to SCR analysis, diving in head first helping out a colleague. I’ve adapted some code by Olivier Gimenez (https://oliviergimenez.github.io/basics_spatial_capturerecapture/).

When I try to build the model using nimbleModel() it stalls at the calculate stage. I’ve left this for several hours with no end in sight. I assume that I have an issue with indexing somewhere, but I cannot find the issue. The data that I have are from live trapping of individuals, so the locations and duration of trapping differs significantly between years, I’ve wondered if that has something to do with it. I attached a very brief script and data, but don’t expect anyone to find the issue for me, a nudge in the right direction would be great! Ultimately the goal is to turn this into a multi-state model.

As a side note, I’m just now looking at the nimbleSCR package and beginning to try to take advantage of the functions in there.

Thanks as always

--

Benjamin Padilla Ph.D
Postdoctoral Research Associate

University of Calgary

Hello all.  I have a question about resetting monitors after an object has been compiled. I believe I am following the instructions correctly, but in so doing, I keep crashing R.

Here is the code that worked to create and run the initial model:

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code=code, constants=consts, data=data, dimensions = dimensions,calculate=T, check=T, inits=I1)

conf  <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, monitors=parms, control = list(adaptInterval = MCMCcontrol$nadapt), thin = MCMCcontrol$nthin, useConjugacy = TRUE)

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel<-compileNimble(Rmodel)

Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

out <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, niter = MCMCcontrol$niter, nburnin = MCMCcontrol$nburn, thin=MCMCcontrol$nthin, nchains=MCMCcontrol$nchains,setSeed = seq(1:nchains), inits = I1, progressBar = TRUE, samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

To reset the monitors, I first redefined “parms”, the vector of variable names  to monitor. The second step (shown below) appeared to work correctly:

conf$setMonitors(parms).

The next step reliably crashes R:

 Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf).

What am I missing?

Thank you!

Rebecca

messages.subject: RE: Open SCR stalls
messages.body_plain:
Hi again, Ben,

If you only want to sample part of the region (e.g. if you are study an islands), you can use Mike Meredith's application (http://mmeredith.net/blog/2016/SECR_patchy_habitat_makeJAGSmask.htm). This will save a lot of computing time. Although written for JAGS, it is very easy to adapt to Nimble in the OpenSCR code. At the same time, makemask does coordinate scaling, which is always convenient.

You can also vectorize some parts of your code, such as:

    SX[i] ~ dunif(xl, xu)

    SY[i] ~ dunif(yl, yu)

    D2[i,1:J] <- pow(SX[i] - trapmat[1:J,1], 2) + pow(SY[i] - trapmat[1:J,2], 2)

    g[i,1:J] <- lam0 * exp(-D2[i,1:J] / (2 * sigma2)) #lam0 activity

    pmean[i,1:J] <- 1 - exp(-g[i,1:J])

    for(j in 1:J) { # loop over all traps

      for (t in 1:T){

        tmp[t,i,j] <- z[i,t] * pmean[i,j]

        y[t,i,j] ~ dbin(tmp[t,i,j], K[t,j]) # K is the number of days a trap was operational

      }

    }

You can build a function (e.g. like GetDetection in https://github.com/benaug) to make the code faster.

To save time, you can use as well:

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code = code,

                      constants = constants,

                      data = data,

                      inits = inits, check=FALSE, calculate=FALSE)

Surely the Nimble team can give you other useful tips.

Best

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marie,

If I follow, after this step

parentNodes <- parentNodes[-which(parentNodes %in% dataNodes)]

parentNodes contains "gamma" and "phi".  And then Istar[1] does not depend on gamma or phi, so it is not included in

nodesToSim <- sirsModel$getDependencies(parentNodes, self = FALSE, downstream = T)

Rstar[1] and Sstar[1] depend on gamma and phi, and then via those nodes Istar[2] and later ones are all in the downstream results.  It's just that Istar[1] starts the sequence and does not depend on gamma or phi.

I need to amend my reply about pi. I was forgetting that the choice to not support pi as a constant in model code, the way it is in R or nimbleFunction code, was deliberate because pi is not uncommonly used as a variable name in models. So instead what I think we should look into is providing a helpful error or warning message.  If one follows the output of nimbleModel and checks sirsModel$initializeInfo(), one can see that pi is indeed part of what is unknown, and this can be a flag that it is not supported as a constant.  But it is somewhat buried.

Best wishes,
Perry

messages.body_plain:
This is an update to the question I posted yesterday.

I think the problem has to do with the fact that I am trying to run nimble after reopening a saved R workspace. All of the objects I expect to be there are indeed present in the workspace. But I get the following errors if I don’t change anything and just try to rerun the model.

When I try Cmcmc$run(niter), I get the following error:

Error in .Call("CALL_MCMC_run", niter, reset, resetMV, time, progressBar,  : C symbol name "CALL_MCMC_run" not in load table

When I try this,

out   <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, niter = MCMCcontrol$niter, nburnin = MCMCcontrol$nburn, thin=MCMCcontrol$nthin, nchains=MCMCcontrol$nchains, setSeed = seq(1:nchains), inits = I1, progressBar = TRUE, samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

I get this error:

Error in .Call(NULL, <pointer: (nil)>, 1L) : first argument must be a string (of length 1) or native symbol reference

Is there a way to rerun a nimble model from a saved workspace without going through the configureMCMC step again? (That is the time consuming part for my model.)

Thank you!

Rebecca Taylor
Research Statistician
Alaska Science Center
U. S. Geological Survey
(907) 786-7004

From: 'Rebecca Taylor' via nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
Sent: Wednesday, March 8, 2023 12:07 PM
To: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [EXTERNAL] resetting monitors after initial compilation

Hello all.  I have a question about resetting monitors after an object has been compiled. I believe I am following the instructions correctly, but in so doing, I keep crashing R.

Here is the code that worked to create and run the initial model:

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code=code, constants=consts, data=data, dimensions = dimensions,calculate=T, check=T, inits=I1)

conf  <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, monitors=parms, control = list(adaptInterval = MCMCcontrol$nadapt), thin = MCMCcontrol$nthin, useConjugacy = TRUE)

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel<-compileNimble(Rmodel)

Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

out <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, niter = MCMCcontrol$niter, nburnin = MCMCcontrol$nburn, thin=MCMCcontrol$nthin, nchains=MCMCcontrol$nchains,setSeed = seq(1:nchains), inits = I1, progressBar = TRUE, samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

To reset the monitors, I first redefined “parms”, the vector of variable names  to monitor. The second step (shown below) appeared to work correctly:

conf$setMonitors(parms).

The next step reliably crashes R:

 Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf).

What am I missing?

Thank you!

Rebecca

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rebecca,

Unfortunately, you cannot save and reload nimble objects (models, MCMCs, etc.). The reason has to do with how objects in C++ are set up and accessed from R.
It's a known shortcoming and one we have been working on a solution for, but it's part of a long-term effort.

-Chris

Hi All,

I've been trying to use MCMC on an SIR-style model, and I've managed to get everything running without errors, but my sampling is very inefficient (see traceplots below). I'm currently using the default "RW sampler", I tried two parameters to "AF_slice" just to see what would happen, and it made the process considerably slower. I'm assuming I need to use more appropriate samplers? But I have no idea how to start thinking about that!

Here is a reproducible version of the code I am using (runs with attached function and C file):

library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)
library(deSolve)
library(nimble)
library(readxl)
library(tidyr)
setwd("C:/Users/dms228/R Scripts/nimble")
source("model1_v9_functions.R")

#######################################################################################
##                                        SET UP                                     ##

Ih0      = N * 0.0007
B0       = 30000000
R0       = 3500000
S0       = N - Io0 - Ih0 - R0

sim.start.date <- as.Date("1989-12-31")

messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I am struggling to get a Cox Proportional Hazard model up
and running in nimble. I am using bugs code for reference that has been
implemented multiple times in other papers, but I am getting an error for
multiple declarations of a node.

Here is the model code:

nimble::nimbleCode({

#n = number of individuals

#t = the time step

for(b in 1:Nbeta){

    beta[b] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)

}

for(i in 1:n){

    for(k in 1:t){

      # risk set = 1 if obs.t >= t

      Y[i,k] <- step(obs.t[i] - t.int <http://t.int>[k] +
eps)

      # counting process jump = 1 if obs.t is
within interval

      dN[i,k] <- Y[i,k] * step(t.int <http://t.int>[k + 1]
- obs.t[i] - eps) * delta[i]

    }

}

# Model

for(k in 1:t){

    for(i in 1:n){

      dN[i,k] ~ dpois(idt[i,k]) # likelihood

      idt[i,k]
<- Y[i,k] * exp(LinearPred[i]) * dL0[k] # intensity

      # linear predictors

      LinearPred[i] <- beta[1]*X[i,1] +
beta[2]*X[i,2] + beta[3]*X[i,3] + beta[4]*X[i,4]

    }

    dL0[k] <- dgamma(0.01, 0.01)

    # Survivor function =
exp(-Integral{l0(u)du})^exp(beta*z)

    S[k] <- pow(exp(-sum(dL0[1:k])),
exp(LinearPred[i] * -0.5))

    }

})

I am getting the multiple declarations
error for dN. I understand that I am defining dN twice; however, I am attempting
to first deterministically define dN in the first chunk then use dN for a likelihood
function as data to estimate idt and the other parameters. I will admit that I
have not run this in winBugs, but the model structure is used in multiple
different papers. Is there anyway to make this work in nimble?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

A few thoughts, though I think #1 may be enough.

1) When you run `my.waic`, I think you need to pass in one of the subsamples matrices not the full matrix. That looks like it works when I try it. Otherwise, you might be calculating WAIC on a bunch of rows with zeros or some such (I haven't looked closely).
2) You can unload DLLs, as described here in the manual <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-progr-with-models.html#clearing-and-unloading-compiled-objects>. That may be a quick and dirty fix.
3) A more comprehensive approach might work as follows. This would involve a deeper dive into the code but if you wanted to do this sort of thing a lot, it might be worth it. The buildWAIC nimblefunction has a `reset` function that resets the summary statistics used in calculating WAIC. I think you can make use of that in combination with setting `lengthConvCheck` to be equal to the number of subsets you want. Then, every X iterations, in the `updateStats` method you can save the current WAIC and reset the summary stats. Note that the ability to have the `WAIC`, `lppd`, `pWAIC` storage objects have length greater than one is intended for assessing Monte Carlo uncertainty when using marginal WAIC, but I think you can repurpose things.

-chris

If by p[i] you mean the zeroProb then, to the best of my knowledge, the beta distribution is not a conjugate prior. This is only true when fitting the zero inflated model with data augmentation https://georgederpa.github.io/teaching/countModels.html .

To get the likelihood just use the dZIP function. dZIP(x=y,lambda=lambda, zeroProb=p) will give the likelihood for lambda and p when observing y. Although I don't know if this will actually work in the model code, but it will definitely work outside it. You should compute these things after running the MCMC anyway, in my view.

messages.subject_clean: Cox Proportional Hazard model - multiple declarations for a node
messages.body_plain:
Anthony, thanks for using nimble, and also for sending this question.

Yes, you're correct that nimble does not allow *both* stochastic (~) and deterministic (<-) declarations of the same node.  Using both would invariably lead to some ambiguity, for example:

x <- a + b
x ~ dnorm(0, 1)

Should the value of x be fixed to be consistently equal to "a + b" ?
If x is not specified as data, then should this non-data node be sampled from a dnorm(0,1) distribution?  Sampling of x would likely be inconsistent with the value "a+b", leading to a contradiction.
If x is specified as data, and a data value is provided, then that value is likely different from the value "a+b", leading to another contradiction.

So, in the design of nimble, we do not allow this case.

I can understand one use-case here, which is the following: As in the example above, you want the value of "a+b" to contribute to the likelihood, being evaluated as compared to a dnorm(0,1) distribution.  In this case, you could achieve this in nimble using a custom distribution, as:

dMyDist <- nimbleFunction(
   run = function(x = double(), theta = double(), log = integer()) {    ## "y" will take the place of "x", and "a+b" will take the place of "theta"
      lp <- dnorm(theta, 0, 1)    ## you could use any distribution here, in your case dpois()
      returnType(double())
      if(log) return(lp) else return(exp(lp))
   }
)

code <- nimbleCode({
   ...
   y ~ dMyDist(theta = a + b)
})

## definitely specify a data value for y, so the model does not try to simulate it
data <- list(y = 0)    ## the data value you provide for y does not matter.  It will be used as "x" in the custom distribution (which is never used)

This code above should get you running, if your desired use-case is the one described above.  Let me know if you need help modifying the code above for your specific model.   for(k in 1:t){
    for(i in 1:n){

So, unless LinearPred is also indexed by k (for example: LinearPred[i,k] <- ...), your model will also result in multiple declarations for LinearPred[i].  It might be a simple matter of changing the nesting of your for-loops a little bit, so the declaration LinearPred[i] only appears in one loop: for(i in 1:n).

messages.subject: Re: ZIP conjugacy and PPOi
messages.body_plain:
To add a little bit from the perspective of nimble's conjugacy system:

Similar to the "registerDistributions(...)" function, we've also contemplated a "registerConjugacy" function, where you could register additional known conjugate relationships (which could involve user-defined distributions, as in your case) with nimble.  Then, they would be detected and handled automatically, just like other conjugacies.  That said, "registerConjugacy" does not exist, so your other best options are:

(a) Manually adding the conjugate relationship you want to the nimble package.  Start by Forking the nimble repository, and adding a definition of your new conjugate relationship to the beginning of MCMC_conjugacy.R <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_conjugacy.R>, following the same pattern as the definitions of the other conjugate relationships defined there. Then build the modified package, and load it from an R session.  Using this approach, nimble would then automatically detect this conjugate relationship in models, dynamically generate the appropriate conjugate sampler, and use it in the MCMC.

(b) Otherwise, you could write your own conjugate sampler function, and assign it manually using functions such as conf$addSampler().

Both approaches have merits.

If you choose to go down either (a) or (b), someone could probably help you.

Option (a) might feel daunting, but honestly if you're ok with forking the repository, and building your own local version of the nimble package, then this approach is way easier, in every way.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I know the MCMC chain will continue from where it left off if I run runMCMC() again. I found it will not keep the existing samples. I would like to ask how I can keep the existing samples. For instance, if I first set niter = 100 and N = number of parameters, it returns 100*N. I re-run runMCMC() again with niter = 50, it returns 50*N, but I want to keep to have 100*N (from 51th to 150th). How can I achieve this goal by runMCMC()?

The reason to do so is that I want to check convergence in the simulation study and save time. If not converged, I extend the MCMC length by window (keep the last 100 samples).

Thanks a lot!

Keith

messages.subject: Re: Continue runMCMC() with existing samples
messages.body_plain:
Good question, Keith.  I'm glad to hear that you find runMCMC() easy to use.  That said, to achieve what it sounds like you're after, you would not use runMCMC().

Instead of:

samples10 <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, niter = 10)   ## generate first 10 samples
## cannot run for 10 more samples using runMCMC

You would use:

Cmcmc$run(10)   ## generate first 10 samples
samples10 <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)
## inspect first 10 samples, contained in samples10 matrix, if you wish
Cmcmc$run(10, reset = FALSE)    ## run for 10 more samples
samples20 <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)   ## extract all 20 samples

Another nuance to mention: when you execute runMCMC(), it "resets" the MCMC algorithm.  Specifically, all adaptive samplers are reset to their initial (pre-adative) state.  If you truly want to "extend an MCMC chain for more samples), then you really need to use the Cmcmc$run(..., reset = FALSE) , which prevents the MCMC from "resetting", and does in fact continue the same MCMC chain.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Continue runMCMC() with existing samples
messages.body_plain:
Great questions, Keith.

I suggest you read Chapter 7 (MCMC) of the NIMBLE User Manual <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-mcmc.html>. This will help answer many of your questions.

Briefly:

1. Both Cmcmc$run() with or without using the reset argument performs adaptive sampling.  The samplers used in nimble - those of which undergo adaptation - are always adapting, unless you disable it using the sampler control list argument "adaptive = FALSE".  The User Manual describes providing control options to samplers, when you configure the MCMC.

Also, implemented as such, you do not need to worry about the adaptation.  You can run the MCMC algorithm for as long as you want, discard whatever initial samples you'd like as burn-in, then safely use the remaining samples for inferences.

2.  Regarding the options you use for runMCMC:

samples <- runMCMC( Cmcmc , niter = 5000, nburnin = 5000, nchains= 2
                                              ,samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE
                                              ,samples=TRUE
                                              ,summary=TRUE
                                              ,WAIC = TRUE
                                              ,setSeed = 1)

You can accomplish the iterations and burnin using:
Cmcmc$run(10000)
Then extract all 10000 samples.
Then drop the first 5000 samples as burnin.

You can accomplish two chains by calling Cmcmc$run() again.

You can calculate the summer metrics using:
samplesSummary(samplesArray)

For WAIC, you will need to enable the WAIC calculations as:
buildMCMC(..., enableWAIC = TRUE).
Then, after running the MCMC, you can later extract the WAIC value using:
Cmcmc$getWAIC()
Note, this will give you the WAIC calculated separately for each chain (calling getWAIC after executing each chain).  If this is a major concern for you, we could describe a work-around to calculate WAIC using the samples from both chains.

For getting the samples as a coda object, use the as.mcmc() and as.mcmc.list() functions from the coda package:
coda::as.mcmc(samplesArray)

I hope this gets you started.  Keep at it.

Daniel

>
> I imagine that I need to tune the MH algorithm with an adaptive algorithm for the FIRST run. For later runs, I simply need to increase the MCMC length without the adaptive MH and burn-in period.
>
> 2. How to keep the sample output format as runMCMC() when I use Cmcmc$run(10)?
>
> In my code, I used (for the FIRST run):
>
> samples <- runMCMC( Cmcmc , niter = 5000, nburnin = 5000, nchains= 2
>                                               ,samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE
>                                               ,samples=TRUE
>                                               ,summary=TRUE
>                                               ,WAIC = TRUE
>                                               ,setSeed = 1)
>
> For later runs, I wonder how can I keep to obtain the same format of the output results ("samples" here) by using Cmcmc$run(5000, reset = FALSE )?
>
> Especially, I run multiple chains (nchains= 2 ), require  samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE , samples=TRUE, summary=TRUE,  WAIC = TRUE, and set random seed. If I just use Cmcmc$run(10), it is unclear to me how to obtain the same output format.
>

> Daniel Turek 在 2023年3月16日 星期四凌晨12:43:03 [UTC+8] 的信中寫道：
> > Good question, Keith.  I'm glad to hear that you find runMCMC() easy to use.  That said, to achieve what it sounds like you're after, you would not use runMCMC().
> >
> > Instead of:
> >
> > samples10 <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, niter = 10)   ## generate first 10 samples
> > ## cannot run for 10 more samples using runMCMC
> >
> > You would use:
> >
> > Cmcmc$run(10)   ## generate first 10 samples
> > samples10 <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)
> > ## inspect first 10 samples, contained in samples10 matrix, if you wish
> > Cmcmc$run(10, reset = FALSE)    ## run for 10 more samples
> > samples20 <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)   ## extract all 20 samples
> >
> > Another nuance to mention: when you execute runMCMC(), it "resets" the MCMC algorithm.  Specifically, all adaptive samplers are reset to their initial (pre-adative) state.  If you truly want to "extend an MCMC chain for more samples), then you really need to use the Cmcmc$run(..., reset = FALSE) , which prevents the MCMC from "resetting", and does in fact continue the same MCMC chain.
> >

messages.body_plain:
I realised that option a) would be easy, as it only would need to add a line to the beta conjugacy chunk. However, I don't know if using the defined dZIP there would work. Also, I dont have experience in forking an building packages.
Option b) would be faster, as would be defined adhoc. However, I have not found any example on Nimble webpage on how to create a Gibbs conjugacy sampler.

El martes, 14 de marzo de 2023 a las 19:57:09 UTC+1, Daniel Turek escribió:
> To add a little bit from the perspective of nimble's conjugacy system:
>
> Similar to the "registerDistributions(...)" function, we've also contemplated a "registerConjugacy" function, where you could register additional known conjugate relationships (which could involve user-defined distributions, as in your case) with nimble.  Then, they would be detected and handled automatically, just like other conjugacies.  That said, "registerConjugacy" does not exist, so your other best options are:
>
> (a) Manually adding the conjugate relationship you want to the nimble package.  Start by Forking the nimble repository, and adding a definition of your new conjugate relationship to the beginning of MCMC_conjugacy.R <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_conjugacy.R>, following the same pattern as the definitions of the other conjugate relationships defined there. Then build the modified package, and load it from an R session.  Using this approach, nimble would then automatically detect this conjugate relationship in models, dynamically generate the appropriate conjugate sampler, and use it in the MCMC.
>
> (b) Otherwise, you could write your own conjugate sampler function, and assign it manually using functions such as conf$addSampler().
>
> Both approaches have merits.
>
> If you choose to go down either (a) or (b), someone could probably help you.
>
> Option (a) might feel daunting, but honestly if you're ok with forking the repository, and building your own local version of the nimble package, then this approach is way easier, in every way.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks John.
The problem is not jumping out at me, so let me suggest some strategies (and/or you can send the data off-list, as you mentioned).
I suspect you're right the issue is in BUGS_modelDef.R.  Some of the code there constructs chunks of R code and then evaluates them to extract information about for loops and sometimes constants.  The error looks like it involves some of that constructed code.
The first thing I would try is to use 'calculate=FALSE' to confirm the error still occurs, which means it has to do with processing the model code to determine the DAG structure (which I think is the case), as opposed to running the custom functions.
Next I would try, to the extent possible, cutting out portions of the model (or, sometimes easier, building up the model from scratch component by component), to narrow down what component introduces the error.
Also I would triple-check that your constants are populated with valid values of correct sizes.  (In the code you sent, Consts$n and Consts$m have not been set, but I'm guessing that was an oversight in putting together the code to send, because you would have hit an error otherwise from that. Or maybe I missed it.)
And I would start poking most at the code with the for loop with 'i' as the indexing variable.  You could even just change that variable name and see if the variable in the error message changes to match.  That would confirm that some code in that loop is the issue.  Now I'm starting to speculate.
And if you're really adventurous, you could set "options(error = recover)" and then when thrown into a browser you will likely be in the source code function "expandContextAndReplacements" (where "context" here refers to the for-loops in which a line of code occurs).  If you open that up, you can see variables to inspect and they might contain clues.  Then you'd be pretty deep into things but that might be of interest to you.
Again, feel free to send the data and reproducible code off-list.
HTH
Perry

messages.subject: Registering truncated distribution with bounds as argument
messages.subject_clean: Registering truncated distribution with bounds as argument
messages.body_plain:
I would like to use a truncated Pareto prior for my Bayesian model, but I couldn't find a way to specify the truncation bounds as parameters of the distribution.

As written in section 12.2.1 of the documentation, the custom distribution must be registered using registerDistributions whenever we want to "provide the range of possible values for a distribution.". While I can create nimble functions to compute the PDF and to sample the distribution with the bounds [xmin, xmax] as arguments, I cannot provide the correct distribution support in the registered distribution:
dpareto <- nimbleFunction( run = function(x = double(0), exponent = double(0), minvalue = double(0), log = integer(0, default = 0)) { returnType(double(0)) log_prob <- log(exponent) + exponent * log(minvalue) - (exponent + 1) * log(x) if (log) return(log_prob) else return(exp(log_prob)) } ) assign("dpareto", dpareto, envir = .GlobalEnv) registerDistributions(list( dpareto = list( BUGSdist = "dpareto(exponent, minvalue)", pqAvail = FALSE, range = c(minvalue, Inf) # minvalue is not a valid parameter here ) ))

I present the usual Pareto distribution here, but eventually I will also provide an upper bound. Is there a way to register a distribution with varying bounds?

Thank you for your time! (Copy of issue #1284 - https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/issues/1284)

messages.subject: step function when x = 0
messages.body_plain: In the user manual (0.4), the 'step' function is defined as returning 0 if x < 0, 1 if x > 0. I think what it returns when x = 0 is ambiguous, right? messages.subject: Re: Registering truncated distribution with bounds as argument
messages.subject_clean: Registering truncated distribution with bounds as argument
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
You should not add the minvalue argument into your user defined distribution. Instead you can specify the range of the distribution via the range argument in the registerDistribution function. For example if the range is 0 to 100 then:
registerDistributions(list(dpareto = list(BUGSdist = "dpareto(args)", range = c(0, 100))))

Hope this helps.

Best wishes,
Wei

>
> As written in section 12.2.1 of the documentation, the custom distribution must be registered using registerDistributions whenever we want to "provide the range of possible values for a distribution.". While I can create nimble functions to compute the PDF and to sample the distribution with the bounds [xmin, xmax] as arguments, I cannot provide the correct distribution support in the registered distribution:
> dpareto <- nimbleFunction( run = function(x = double(0), exponent = double(0), minvalue = double(0), log = integer(0, default = 0)) { returnType(double(0)) log_prob <- log(exponent) + exponent * log(minvalue) - (exponent + 1) * log(x) if (log) return(log_prob) else return(exp(log_prob)) } ) assign("dpareto", dpareto, envir = .GlobalEnv) registerDistributions(list( dpareto = list( BUGSdist = "dpareto(exponent, minvalue)", pqAvail = FALSE, range = c(minvalue, Inf) # minvalue is not a valid parameter here ) ))
>
> I present the usual Pareto distribution here, but eventually I will also provide an upper bound. Is there a way to register a distribution with varying bounds?

messages.subject: Re: step function when x = 0
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for raising the question Quresh and for the reply, Matt.

I want to point out also that a lot of nimble's functions have aliases with a "nim" prefix, e.g. "nimStep" for "step".  nimbleFunction code is automatically modified to call those aliases (and you can program with them directly if you wish).  So, to see the uncompiled version of `step`, you can type `nimStep`, which gives

> nimStep
function (x)
ifelse(x >= 0, 1L, 0L)

so indeed the x==0 case should return 1.

Cheers,
Perry

Hi there,

I am hoping that someone could offer advice on model selection in nimble for a capture-recapture-recovery model in which I am exploring fixed and random effects on survival and detection of birds.

I have been using WAIC values to compare different model structures. In some contexts,  models exhibit markedly lower WAIC values than alternatives but parameters (especially SDs for random effects) show poor mixing across chains (and largish Rhat values).

I am wondering how meaningful WAIC is in this context and whether I should be prioritizing use of WAIC or convergence of parameter estimates across chains when thinking about model development and selection.

Apologies if this is a straightforward question. I am new to NIMBLE and Bayesian frameworks for developing and comparing models. Happy to offer more details if it would be helpful.

Many thanks,

Justin

messages.subject: Re: WAIC and/or convergence of parameter estimates
messages.subject_clean: WAIC and/or convergence of parameter estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Justin,

You want to make sure you have a reasonable sample from the posterior (i.e., decent mixing) before you try to assess differences in WAIC for different models. The WAIC values will not be reliable for a poorly mixed chain for a given model -- WAIC averages over the model performance for each sample of the parameter vector. Then you would ideally choose a model that gives better WAIC than other models. That said, it may be the case that for some model it is very hard to get good mixing -- but ideally one wouldn't have to discard models because one is unable to fit them.

-Chris

messages.subject: Re: printSamplersByType(ind) : something went wrong
messages.body_plain:
Dan, thanks for raising this issue, and also sending your example off-list.

For anyone interested, the problem was stemming from using *both* variable names "x_y" and also "x.y" in model code.  This won't cause any problems with the nimble model object, or the correct execution of the MCMC.  But, the regular expressions being used in printSamplersByType were interpreting the "." as a regular expression wildcard, and thus matching variable names incorrectly.

A patch is available on the development branch of nimble.  Until the next release, this can be installed and used as:

remove.packages('nimble')
library(remotes)
remotes::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'devel', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
library(nimble)

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Use list as constants
messages.body_plain:
Keith, great question.

Unfortunately, there is no support for providing lists (or lists of lists) as elements of the constants, data, or initial values lists.

I don't entirely understand what you're trying to do, in terms of "indices (with different lengths) to indicate the parameter locations in the model", but if you mean different models, where "a" takes on a variety of different numeric vectors of indices, of varying lengths, and you're thinking of something like:

constants <- list(
    a = list(
        c(1,2,3),
        c(1,2,3,4,5),
        c(1,2,3,4,5,6,7)
    )
)

then nimble does not support this.  One approach would be building different model objects, each with its own constants list, for example:

constants <- list(
    a = c(1,2,3)
)

If you wanted to reuse the same model object for repeated simulations, which would be understandable, then you could build the model to allow for the maximum possible length of "a", for example, and then limit the extent to which the elements of "a" are used via some other variable in the model.  In this case, you'd want to provide all these values in the initial values list (rather than the constants list), so they can be modified after building the model.

I hope this helps,
Daniel

This error usually means that the number of indices (e.g "dist[i, k, t]" has 3 indices: i, k and t) for some variable is not completely consistent somewhere in the code and/or the constants, inits or data (e.g. if somewhere dist appears with only 2 indices). messages.subject_clean: Help to solve the "Dynamic index out of bounds" -warning in runCrossValidate
messages.body_plain:
Hi Antti,

In this context, I think you may want to hold out all the observations for each individual together, rather than randomly holding out individual-time point values. If one does the latter, one would have to think about what it means to not see one of the time points for an individual - but that seems unnatural given the meaning of an observation in this context as indicating if an individual is observed or not. So I think the problem is ultimately arising from the nature of the data.

My suggestion would be to write a `foldFunction` that does the hold-out at the individual level. I suspect the problem will go away if you do that.

-chris

messages.subject: Re: Segfault using HMC and is AD fixing model's constants
messages.subject_clean: Segfault using HMC and is AD fixing model's constants
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for using nimbleHMC, and also sending your question.

A very short answer would be: it's not apparent offhand what's going wrong, and to really figure it out, we'd need a reproducible example.  If you'd prefer to send that (model code, data, etc) off-list, then that's no problem at all.

No, only populating half of the values in the adjacency matrix is not a problem.  The HMC sampler will only access and use the values in the parts you access inside the for-loops.

That said: you said that you "only iterate on the lower half of it.... the rest of the matrix is not initialized because of this", but a quick inspection of the for-loops in your code makes it appear like (instead) you only iterate on the upper half of it.  So, perhaps there's something going wrong here (providing values for the wrong half of the adjacency matrix), that might be causing this problem.  It might be worth a look at that.

Regarding your second question: If by "ignores their gradient evaluation" you mean "ignores the gradient evaluation of the custom-written nimble functions entirely", then no, gradients of these functions are not ignored, but rather algebraically derived (via automatic differentiation), while using the values of the constant arguments you provided.  Or, if by "ignores their gradient evaluation", you mean the "ignores the partial derivatives of the custom-written nimble functions w.r.t. the constant-valued arguments", then yes, automatic differentiation is not applied to the constant-valued arguments, much the same as it would not be applied to an argument which is hard-coded as a number (say, 5).  The gradient (partial derivatives) of the function are only calculated w.r.t. continuous-valued non-constant arguments, as is necessary for HMC sampling.

Cheers, keep at it,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Keith, I'm not exactly sure about the application, but the following does the same thing in somewhat less code:

K <- 4
la_index_list <- lapply(1:K, function(k) nimbleType(name = paste0('v',k), type = 'double', dim = 2))
la_index_list_def <- nimbleList(la_index_list)
argList <- lapply(1:K, function(k) combn(1:K,k))
names(argList) <- paste0('v', 1:K)
la_index <- do.call(la_index_list_def$new, argList)

As for your second question, unfortunately no, you need to use the names (e.g., "v1" or "v2") to access the elements.

Another approach to doing this, for variable length K and access using index number, could be using a nimbleFunctionList, where each element in the nimbleFunctIonList is a nimbleFunction with one member data element (to hold the 2x2 matrices), and a method called (for example) getMatrix.  Then, you could access the K matices as:

my_nimbleFunctionList[[1]]$getMatrix()
my_nimbleFunctionList[[2]]$getMatrix()
## etc...

Hope this helps,
Daniel
